q: What is meant by the Preamble?
a: The Preamble is the introduction to the Constitution. It states the source of authority (We, the people of India), the nature of the state (Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic), its objectives (Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity) and the date of adoption (26 November 1949).

q: Write a short note on the Select Committee.
a: A Select Committee is a small group of members of Parliament appointed to examine a particular Bill or matter in detail; the idea comes from the Westminster system. Under Rule 125 of the Rajya Sabha rules a member may move that a Bill be referred to a select committee. The quorum is one-third of its members, the chairman has a casting vote in a tie, and it may form sub-committees.

q: Write a short note on Sankaralinganar.
a: Sankaralinganar (born 1895, Manmalai Medu, Virudhunagar) was a Gandhian freedom fighter who joined the Congress in 1917 and took part in the Salt March of 1930. From 27 July 1956 he fasted at Virudhunagar with 12 demands, chiefly renaming Madras State as Tamil Nadu, and died on the 76th day (13 October 1956). The state was renamed Tamil Nadu on 14 January 1969.

q: Write about the structure of the Tamil Nadu State Legislature.
a: Tamil Nadu has a unicameral legislature: the Governor and the Legislative Assembly. The Assembly has 234 elected members (189 general and 45 reserved constituencies). The Governor earlier nominated one Anglo-Indian member under Article 333 (ended in 2020). The first Madras Legislative Assembly met on 3 May 1952. The Legislative Council was abolished in 1986.

q: Bring out the significance of the Public Accounts Committee.
a: The Public Accounts Committee examines the accounts of government spending and the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General, ensuring that money granted by Parliament is spent as intended. Its Chairperson is appointed by the Speaker from among its members; since 1967-68 an Opposition member is usually made Chairperson, which strengthens financial accountability of the executive.

q: Write a brief note on the composition of the Constituent Assembly.
a: Formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), roughly one seat per 10 lakh population. Total 389: 292 from the provinces, 4 from Chief Commissioners' provinces and 93 from the princely states. Provincial seats were divided among Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs in proportion to population and filled by members of the Provincial Assemblies through proportional representation by single transferable vote. Princely state members were nominated by the rulers. After Partition the strength fell to 299; 284 members signed the Constitution.

q: Write a short note on Indian citizenship.
a: Part II (Articles 5-11) of the Constitution deals with citizenship, and the Citizenship Act, 1955 governs its acquisition and loss. India has single citizenship. Citizenship can be acquired by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory, and lost by renunciation, termination or deprivation. The Act also provides for Overseas Citizens of India (OCI).

q: Bring out the meaning, functions and importance of a Constitution.
a: A constitution is the body of basic rules by which a state is constituted and governed. Functions: it sets out the basic rules for coordination among members of the state, allocates power among the organs of government, limits government power, protects rights, defines citizenship and centre-state relations. Importance: it is the fundamental law of the land, gives people a political identity and empowers government to build a just society.

q: Trace the making of the Indian Constitution.
a:
1. The idea of a Constituent Assembly was first put forward by M.N. Roy (1934); the Congress demanded it in 1935 and the British accepted it in the August Offer (1940).
2. The Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), elected indirectly by the Provincial Assemblies.
3. First meeting: 9 December 1946, with Dr Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary Chairman; Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected President on 11 December 1946.
4. Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946 (adopted 22 January 1947).
5. The Drafting Committee under Dr B.R. Ambedkar was set up on 29 August 1947.
6. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 after 2 years 11 months 18 days; members signed it on 24 January 1950.
7. It came into force on 26 January 1950.

q: Explicate the parliamentary type of democracy in India.
a:
1. Under Article 79 Parliament consists of the President and two Houses, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People).
2. Bicameral: the Upper House represents the states, the Lower House the people.
3. The President is the nominal executive; the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers are the real executive.
4. Ministers must be members of Parliament and are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; they stay in office only while they enjoy its confidence.
5. Parliament controls the executive through questions, debates, motions and committees such as the Public Accounts Committee.
6. Disagreement between the Houses on ordinary bills is settled by a joint sitting called by the President (not for money or amendment bills).

q: Give a detailed account of the sources of the Indian Constitution.
a:
1. Government of India Act, 1935: federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary, public service commissions, emergency provisions, administrative details.
2. Britain: parliamentary government, single citizenship, rule of law, cabinet system, legislative procedure, prerogative writs.
3. USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, impeachment of the President, removal of judges, Vice-President.
4. Ireland: Directive Principles of State Policy.
5. Canada: federation with a strong centre, residuary powers with the centre, appointment of Governors by the centre, advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
6. Australia: Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce, joint sitting.
7. Weimar Germany: suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency.
8. USSR: Fundamental Duties, ideal of social, economic and political justice.
9. France: Republic; liberty, equality, fraternity.
10. South Africa: amendment procedure, election of Rajya Sabha members.

q: Elucidate the salient features of the Indian Constitution.
a:
1. Longest written constitution in the world.
2. Drawn from many sources.
3. A blend of rigidity and flexibility.
4. Sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic.
5. Parliamentary system of government.
6. Federal system with a unitary bias (quasi-federal).
7. Single citizenship.
8. Universal adult franchise (18 years).
9. Independent and integrated judiciary with judicial review.
10. Fundamental Rights (Part III), Directive Principles (Part IV) and Fundamental Duties (Part IVA).
11. Emergency provisions.
12. Balance between parliamentary sovereignty and judicial review.
